headline.main: The American War: U.S. War Veterans Search for Personal Peace in Vietnam
headline.social: The American War: U.S. War Veterans Search for Personal Peace in Vietnam

intro: Fifty years after the end of the war, a group of U.S. veterans spent two weeks traveling through Vietnam by bus. They once came as soldiers. Now, they are searching for forgiveness.
text:
It’s the 11th day of the trip, a hot, humid morning. Chickens cluck in the yard and the smell of burnt wood hangs in the air as the former American soldier pulls off his sandals and hesitantly enters the house barefoot. The last time he was in Vietnam, he was young and heavily armed. Today, 55 years after his return from the jungle, Craige Edgerton is an old man.
Inside, a young man is lying on a woven grass mat beneath a thin blanket, his head propped up on two pillows. His limbs are emaciated, his back is crooked, and his eyes are sunken into his face. He has been paralyzed since birth. Only his eyes are moving, glancing around the room.
Edgerton takes the man’s thin hand. He felt the man’s soft skin, as he would later relate, and thought: "A hand that has never been used.” Then, their gazes meet. Edgerton glances away and stumbles back out the door.
Outside, he sinks down on a low wall, glasses hanging from a strap around his neck, his shoulders slumped. He takes a deep breath, but it doesn’t help.
The memories come flooding back to him anyway. The sandbags, the bunkers, the bare hilltops. Artillery guns jutting up into the air as lights flash across the sky.
Edgerton buries his face in his hands – and cries.
At this moment, it is 1969 all over again for him, war all around. Edgerton was one of around 2.7 million American soldiers sent to Vietnam by the United States. As a lieutenant, he commanded six howitzers, though he never actually fired one himself, he says. He just sat in the bunker, headphones on, and passed along the orders. Canon one, fire. Canon four, fire. But exactly that is the problem.
Projectiles from a 105 mm howitzer fly for several kilometers. So far that the men who fire the guns usually never see where they strike.
"We didn’t ever know what we were firing at. We just pulled the trigger. Today, I think: Holy crap. How many people did I kill? How many soldiers? How many civilians?”
Those questions are the reason why he was in the parking lot of the Hanoi airport, with his trolly and backpack, in the middle of October, 11 days before his flashback and half a century after his military service. A tall, tanned man with broad shoulders bent slightly forward. In front of him, a tour bus is waiting. Behind him is a 20-hour flight from California to Hanoi via Taiwan.
He is now 78 years old, and this is his first trip back to Vietnam since the end of the war. One leg drags slightly as he boards the bus and the driver leans over to give him a hand.
Seventeen people are traveling with him, including eight Vietnam veterans, members of their families and others. On this tour, which has been organized by Veterans for Peace, the Americans will spend two weeks crisscrossing the country, from Hanoi in the north to Ho Chi Minh City in the south – right across the 17th parallel, which once divided Vietnam into two separate countries.
They will visit orphanages and cemeteries where their former enemies are buried. Speak with Vietnamese veterans, swim in the South China Sea and talk about the war during long bus rides. About what Vietnam did to them – and what they did to Vietnam.
This year marks the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War. Between 1955 and 1975, around 58,000 American soldiers died in the violence, along with an estimated 2 million Vietnamese. The communist north fought against the capitalist south – a proxy war pitting the great powers of the era against each other: The Soviet Union and China on one side, the U.S. on the other. It was a war that polarized an entire generation, even in countries that were uninvolved. In West Germany, the 1968-generation demanded an end to imperialism. In East Germany, people donated blood for their socialist brothers and sisters in North Vietnam.
In the U.S., meanwhile, photographer Nick Ut won the 1973 Pulitzer Prize for his black-and-white snapshot of nine-year-old Phan Thi Kim Phuc, naked, her skin in tatters, following a napalm attack.
Vietnam was also the first war that the U.S. lost.
Saigon fell on April 30, 1975, and the south and north were reunited under a communist government. A poor country had defeated the world’s strongest military power.
The U.S. had done everything in its power to win the war. The Americans dropped more bombs during the Vietnam War than during the entirety of World War II, and they deployed a weapon that would continue to haunt the region for many years after the guns had fallen silent: herbicides that didn’t just strip the trees of leaves, but which also poisoned people – the population of Southeast Asia and America’s own soldiers. Agent Orange, the most infamous of the defoliants, drove up cancer rates. Women suffered stillbirths, or their babies were disabled, some with six fingers on one hand.
The Vietnam War changed the way the world viewed the U.S. – and the way the U.S. saw itself, transforming the self-image of a nation that had been convinced of its own infallibility.
The veterans of that war weren’t the first generation of Americans to go to war. But they were the first to wonder whether it was right.
Which is why Edgerton and the others have returned.
In Hanoi, the bus full of Americans rolls across the Red River, which flows through the city. Outside, the heat shimmers over the rooftops, inside, the air conditioning hums. In front of the windshield, three flags sway in unison each time the bus hits a bump, almost as though they were never enemies: the American flag, the Vietnamese flag and the flag of the Communist Party. Among the passengers is a steelworker from Oakland, who arrived in Vietnam before most of the soldiers back then in order to build the infrastructure necessary for the operation, including barracks, fuel tanks and hangars. There is a former munitions specialist from New York City. And an infantryman from San José, who had to watch as his comrade was gunned down by an enemy sniper.
And then there is Edgerton, who is also from San José, California, with a dogeared notebook on his lap full of notes and ideas for poems.
He has come with his wife, and they sometimes point things out to each other that they see outside the window, like the red flags with the hammer and sickle hanging from the lampposts. Or the high rises that stretch so far into the sky that they have to crane their necks to see the tops. For many years, says Edgerton, he didn’t want to admit it – but back then, he had been eager to go to war.
He grew up in Texas, where they would play out World War II on the beach as children, using sticks for guns. Soldiers shooting at German Nazis, the good guys beating the bad guys. That’s how he imagined his military service when he was 19 and enlisted in the Marines, purportedly the toughest branch of the U.S. military, destined for the riskiest of missions.
"Wow,” the infantryman up front calls out. "They have Kentucky Fried Chicken!”
It is the first insight from this trip: America may have lost the war, but capitalism emerged victorious in the end.
None of the new arrivals have ever seen Hanoi before. The city was enemy territory during the war, the realm of Ho Chi Minh, the leader of the communist north. The only Americans who came to Hanoi were downed bomber pilots taken into captivity.
It sounds like a crazy idea: returning to the place that haunts you. But Chuck Searcy, an 80-year-old in a straw hat and a blazer that’s a bit too big for him, believes it is the best decision veterans can make. He sways down the center aisle, microphone in one hand and the other gripping the overhead racks to steady himself. "Welcome back to Vietnam,” he says. "You’ll be surprised at how gracious people are.”
Searcy also served in Vietnam, but he was never sent into combat, just like many Americans who were stationed in the country. He was based in Saigon and analyzed the fighting on behalf of a military intelligence agency. Much of his work was focused on producing numbers that "made it seem as though the U.S. was winning.” Almost 30 years later, he boarded a plane back to Vietnam because he wanted to know what the country looked like in times of peace. A crazy idea?
He was charmed by the small alleyways and French colonial villas of Hanoi. So he stayed, exploring on his bicycle and helping Vietnamese war veterans obtain prosthetics. In 2000, he helped convince Bill Clinton to visit Vietnam as the first U.S. president since the end of the war. And at some point, he started leading American veterans through the erstwhile "Green Hell.”
There was a time when Searcy was afraid for his life in Vietnam. Today, he finds the idea of dying here rather pleasant.
"When I returned home from the war, I was angry and confused,” he tells the others. He says he felt it was his duty to help rectify the damage that had been done. Soon, he realized that by doing his part to repair relations between the U.S. and Vietnam, he was also repairing himself at the same time. He promises the men on the bus that they will have a similar experience: "Everyone goes back with their lives changed for the better.”
That is the idea behind this trip: Those who experience the new Vietnam will find it easier to forget the old Vietnam. Those who help mend the wounds of war heal their own. Every participant pays $1,000 on top of their travel expenses. Over the course of 10 trips since 2012, that has added up to more than $230,000 in donations. Veterans for Peace supports orphanages, victims of Agent Orange and hospitals. It is an attempt to make amends.
Outside the bus, women in bright blue and red dresses are pushing strollers through the park. They munitions specialist from New York watches them. Today is the first time he is really seeing Vietnam. As a 20-year-old, he spent a year here with the Air Force, loading long-range bombers with ammunition on the tarmac. When he did see locals, it was often through barbed wire.
One time, says Searcy, a veteran called one day before the trip was set to start: "I can’t do it,” he said. Soon afterwards, though, he was standing in the Hanoi airport – a bulky man sobbing as slender Vietnamese patted him on the back and said: "It’s okay. America and Vietnam are friends now.”
Searcy was far from the first American veteran to return. Back in the 1980s, doctors would send veterans back to Vietnam to tour the claustrophobic tunnels that had contributed to their trauma. Long-haired men spoke of healing, saying that Vietnam was the country where their childhood had ended – and returning marked their rebirth as men.
Now, with their hair having turned gray and their backs bent, many veterans are once again feeling a need to come back. The erstwhile soldiers know that they don’t have much time left.
In the evening, Edgerton is sitting in the breakfast room of the hotel. He sets a white binder on the table containing the first draft of a book about traumatized soldiers he is writing together with other veterans.
He describes his arrival in Vietnam in April 1969, though he sometimes isn’t certain that things happened exactly how he remembers them or if his memory is simply filling the gaps with images. "I have this scene in my mind of a Jeep bringing me to the demilitarized zone. Vietnamese women are walking along the side of the road.” The previous year, North Vietnamese troops and the Viet Cong had launched a surprise attack against a number of cities and military bases in the south. In Paris, the first peace talks had begun, though they would continue for years with no success. When he arrived at the base, says Edgerton, the battalion commander didn’t look him in the eye. He was probably thinking, says Edgerton: "Here comes another fresh young lieutenant that we’re probably going to send home in a body bag.”
The war seemed like a great adventure to him, and it was for a while. On their military base, the soldiers would fill empty ammunition crates with sand and use them to build huts, called "hootches” by the troops. Down in the valleys, giant leeches crawled through tall elephant grass, so sharp that it could slice through skin. They never saw the enemy. They stayed up on their hill, bare-chested because of the heat, a few teenagers and young men firing artillery into the jungle. Sometimes, they would go for a swim in the lake.
The problems began later. "Bang,” says Edgerton, slamming his hand on the table.
More than 30 years after the war, he was standing in front of the shelves in a grocery store when a palette crashed to the floor behind him. Edgerton immediately threw himself down behind the shopping cart, hands covering his ears as if he was under fire.
"Alcohol, nightmares, failed relationships. Everyone knows the stories of veterans who lost control of their lives,” he says. He didn’t consider himself to be among the problem cases. His second marriage was happy, and he had two daughters and then grandchildren. In his free time, he would go birdwatching in national parks.
But that wasn’t the end of it. During a business lunch, he threw himself to the ground when an airplane passed overhead. A war movie sent him into a crying fit. And then there was this incredible anger with the government. Despite completing a degree in economics, he long preferred to run a small store selling picture frames. When others sang patriotic songs, he would remain silent in protest.
Another member of the tour group compares suppressed war memories with a bottle of mineral water that has been shaken up. "Nothing happens for a long time, but all it takes is one little thing and the lid comes off and – sssssshhh.”
Forty-seven years after the war, at age 70, Edgerton was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). He started therapy, and for the first time, he spoke about what he had seen – and what he might have done.
He pauses. There are memories he doesn’t like talking about. But he ultimately does so anyway. There was this one time when a booby trap tore a soldier’s leg off and Edgerton was charged with leading the evacuation. The helicopter couldn’t land in the dark and they heard the man’s screaming through the night, he says. Edgerton says he doesn’t know if the man survived or not. Often, he says, he sees the "empty look” of a comrade in front of him that they found naked in the forest covered in flies. He had apparently gone mad.
In his binder, there is a note on which Edgerton has written down why he wanted to return to Vietnam. "I hope I can reduce my feelings of guilt and anger.”
But it’s like peeling an onion, he says. "Whenever I think I found the last layer, there’s more.”
On the morning of the third day, they met with Vietnamese officials. Edgerton was sitting at a long wooden table, the walls paneled in dark red, a bust of Ho Chi Minh behind him. The microphone crackled as Edgerton’s voice echoed through the room. "I left Vietnam 55 years ago this month,” he says. "And I don’t understand how the Vietnamese people have been so forgiving. Why aren’t the Vietnamese angry with us?”
A man in a dark green suit rose to his feet and said what the veterans would hear over and over again during this trip: "We are convinced that many U.S. soldiers didn’t want to fight. They were following orders.”
Outside, a woman is pushing a bicycle in front of the bus loaded down with dragon fruit and bananas. Edgerton rests his forehead against the window, thinking about why the Vietnamese show no anger. Because of Buddhism? Because most of them are too young to have experienced the war? Or because it was just one of the country’s many battles for independence?
The Vietnamese call the Vietnam War the "American War.”
And if the Vietnamese forgive him, does that mean that he is allowed to forgive himself? He rubs his eyes with the heels of his hands. "I want to forgive myself,” he says. "But it’s hard.”
Before he went off to war, he had a party together with his friends and girlfriend. If he returned, it would be as the savior of the world. Or so he thought. Seven months later, he was back in Texas – but found himself confronted with incomprehension. It was 1969. The U.S. had just learned of the My Lai Massacre, during which a company of U.S. troops slaughtered an entire village. In Woodstock, 400,000 hippies celebrated peace, love and music. And Muhammad Ali had just refused the draft, saying: "The real enemy of my people is right here” and not in Vietnam.
For the liberals in the U.S., Edgerton was a killer. For the conservatives, he was a loser.
After completing his military service in 1971, he threw away his uniform and his medals, grew a moustache and let his hair grow long. He ignored the news, and when somebody spoke of Vietnam, he acted as though he had never been there. If his country wanted to forget the war, he would do the same.
Many years later, he watched a documentary, and he understood what had long since become public knowledge. That the U.S. had officially gone to war to support South Vietnam and to stop the spread of communism – but that Washington had realized early on that the campaign was hopeless. Nevertheless, the U.S. military continued sending young men and women to Southeast Asia, continued to drop bombs and continued to deploy napalm. Henry Kissinger, who would later become U.S. secretary of state, privately admitted that no vital national interests were at stake in Vietnam – aside from America’s credibility. "The government knew that the war between North and South Vietnam wasn’t a communist plot to take over the world,” says Edgerton. "They lied to us.”
Have you ever heard the term moral injury, he asks? It’s when a person performs their duties but their actions violate their own values. Edgerton says: "I grew up in the Catholic Church. I was raised with certain morals and principles. I joined the Marine Corps to defend my country. I wanted to do the right thing. But did the wrong thing.”
According to a study conducted by the U.S. Department of Veteran Affairs, 15 percent of the 2.7 million soldiers sent to Vietnam suffered from PTSD in 1983. Around 58,000 U.S. troops lost their lives in the war. More than 22,000 committed suicide afterwards.
Perhaps it is because the Vietnam War was not seen as a "just war.” Because it’s one thing to kill a soldier. But another thing when you realize you have done so for the wrong reasons.
"One memory keeps popping up,” says Edgerton. One day, he says, it was his turn to patrol the perimeter of the base. In the dense brush, where the American mortar shells usually fell, he happened across a woman with her children. "The sight of them tore me up. They were trying to make a living while we were blowing up their world.” Today, he says: "Maybe my feelings of guilt started back then.”
There’s a jolt, the tour group’s plane touches down and rolls across the tarmac of the airport in Da Nang. Here, where the South China Sea meets the dark green mountains of central Vietnam, is the former location of one of the largest U.S. bases during the war. In 1965, the first U.S. soldiers went ashore on the beach here.
At dusk, a beer on the table next to him, Edgerton begins showing photos from the war on his tablet. "Here,” he says, "that was great.” In the picture, a shirtless Edgerton with a radio around his neck can be seen kneeling on the hilltop of their fire support base, rolling hills behind him. He has pleasant memories of the evenings, when the temperature cooled off, the monkeys chattered in the treetops and the sun sank below the horizon over Laos.
Edgerton leans back. Half of the trip is now over. "It’s impressive how the Vietnamese have turned their country around,” he says. He has met with young Vietnamese and with politicians, and he has shaken hands with a former captain in the Vietnamese military, his erstwhile enemy.
The encounters have impressed him, but he has also occasionally come away frustrated. Before embarking on the trip, he had noted down a few questions he wanted to ask people: How do you see the war? How do you speak to your families about your memories? What is on your mind?
But no real discussions have developed. Is it because of the language barrier? Or because the Vietnamese prefer speaking about anything but the past? For the American veterans, the war is still very much present, but for many Vietnamese, it is simply history.
Most are too young to have experienced the war themselves, and at school, they learn what the Communist Party wants them to learn: "We won. Today, we are a country that looks to the future.”
When the guns finally fell silent, Vietnam was one of the poorest countries in the world. Today, it is a repressive yet economically successful one-party state. Half of all Samsung mobile phones are produced here, and it exports more pepper to the U.S. than any other country.
During the day, as they drove through Da Nang, Edgerton sat in the middle of the bus. Behind him was the steelworker from Oakland, who arrived in Da Nang early on, in 1965, to help build the infrastructure of war.
The day before, as he was examining a map, the steelworker thought about renting a car and driving to the building that used to house the old exchange, where troops could buy things they needed. Now, looking out the window, he realizes just how silly that idea was. On China Beach, where he used to go swimming, diggers are making way for the next vacation resort. Mopeds and electric buses are zooming down four-lane roads. Even the forest on the hilltops only looks like a jungle from a distance. Today, the hills are mostly covered by acacia trees cultivated for the furniture industry.
It is good for Edgerton to see a country that is completely different from the one in his memories. Maybe, he will soon be able to really believe what he said many years ago during a therapy session: "I was in the war. I was not the war.”
Three days later, that lightness has vanished.
On that day – 10 days into their trip – Edgerton finds himself in a visitor’s center in Quang Tri, the northernmost province of former South Vietnam. He is surrounded by barbed wire, artificial limbs and metal detectors. He watches as a Vietnamese man on crutches limps around in front of a group of second-graders. The man’s right eye is scarred shut and one of his arms comes to an end below the elbow.
"What is that?” the man asks the children in their red-and-beige uniforms as he gestures to a screen on the wall.
"Hand grenades!” the children call out."And that?”"Mortar shells!”
The veterans are visiting Project Renew, a bomb clearance service that Searcy founded. Since 2001, the service has dug 120,000 duds out of the reddish-brown soil of Quang Tri. The demilitarized zone, which sliced Vietnam in half, ran through here among the rugged hills and tropical forests. Nowhere was the American bombing campaign more intense.
An American war reporter who flew over Quang Tri in 1972 described the province as a panorama of craters. "As far as we could determine, not a single permanent building, urban or rural, remained intact: no private dwellings, no schools, no libraries, no churches or pagodas; and no hospitals.” Edgerton was stationed here.
"Do you know how I lost my arm,” the man with the crutches asks? He says he was 10 years old when he and two cousins found a cluster bomb – as small as a tennis ball. He threw a rock at it to see what would happen. His cousins, he said, were killed in the ensuing explosion, but he survived.
"What should you do if you find a bomb?” the man asks the children. "Don’t touch it! Get help!” the children call out before then chanting the emergency number in their bright voices.
Black-and-white photos on the walls depict B-52 bombers and people fleeing. Edgerton and the other veterans move from picture to picture. A girl with a ponytail wants to show the Americans what she has learned. She points to a rusted piece of munition. "Bom chum,” she says, the Vietnamese word for cluster bomb. Edgerton seems troubled. This is, he says, the point of the trip after all: to see what America has done.
An estimated 10 percent of American bombs didn’t detonate. According to the Vietnamese government, 40,000 people were killed by such duds by 2014, and 60,000 were injured, many of them children.
On the way back to the bus, Edgerton stops in front of an artillery shell, the exact type he used to help target in the jungle. Someone has placed a dried flower in the empty shell. He takes a picture.
War and peace in a single image.
Does he feel responsible when he sees all these explosives? "Oh yes,” he whispers.
Back on the bus, everyone is silent
There are those who are critical of such trips to Vietnam. The Australian historian Mia Hobbs, who wrote her doctoral thesis on Vietnam veterans who return to Vietnam, says: "It’s a caring role that has been forced on the Vietnamese in their own country.”
Word has spread in the U.S. that Vietnam welcomes veterans with open arms. The veterans travel to the country and speak about their pain while the Vietnamese hold their hands. And the Americans are finally able to find themselves in the role they wanted back then: conflicted heroes.
In his notebook, Edgerton has written down a sentence he heard during their travels and now recites it: "Vietnam is a country, not a war.” It is something that young Vietnamese in particular are likely to say. It sometimes bothers them to be reduced to a terrible memory. The sentence has changed Edgerton’s perspective. "While I felt sorry for myself all those years, the Vietnamese were rebuilding their country.”
Before his departure, his therapist asked Edgerton what would make for a successful trip. His answer: "If the last peel of the onion fell.”
He doesn’t have much time left. It is day 11 and the group is headed off to Ho Chi Minh City, formerly Saigon, the next day, and from there, they will be flying back to the U.S. But then, it happens, in the Gio Linh District, a place where Edgerton wasn’t expecting to find the core of the onion. Why here, though? Perhaps because he used to be stationed here. But perhaps also because something had to happen to ensure that this trip was not made in vain.
It rained in the morning and the mountains are shimmering deep blue. Farmers are wading through rice fields flooded by the monsoon rains. The bus stops on the side of the road and Edgerton and the others get out and walk along a path to a house made of bricks. Ha Thi Hoang is waiting for them on the veranda, a slender woman with strong arms. Rainwater drips from the corrugated metal roof. She says she has been awake since dawn, nervous because she had been told how big the Americans are and there would be so many of them in her small home.
Stickers from two Korean aid agencies are stuck to the outside wall, but none from America. Ha Thi Hoang wants to change that, which is why she invited the veterans to come for a visit.
Her son suffers from "third generation effects of Agent Orange,” she explains to the men and women standing in the rain-soaked courtyard. "I receive a state allowance, but it’s not even enough for his diapers.” Her son is 29. And unable to speak.
Edgerton takes down her words. Through the open door, he sees a shelf with a report card from the 11th grade and the photo of a girl. He writes down what Ha Thi Hoang now says: "My daughter is our best hope.”
Edgerton takes off his sandals and enters the home. The young man is lying in bed, his hair waving from the fan. Edgerton grabs his hand – and then it happens.
He hurries outside and slumps down on the wall.
Later, on the bus, he is slouched in his seat. The others are visiting a cemetery for fallen Vietnamese soldiers. "When I looked into the young man’s eyes,” he says, "this scene exploded in my head.” Lights in the sky, the bunker, the dust in the air – suddenly, it all came rushing back. "It was like something I was holding onto was being washed away.”
A cleansing sensation?
He thinks for a bit. "Forgiving.” He pauses. "I know it sounds weird.” It was like a discharge of energy, he says. It went pop, pop – and then: "Another layer of this anger was released. Maybe the forgiveness I have been searching for. It was something I never experienced before.”
What happened to Edgerton in that moment – or what he believes to have happened – sounds fantastical, almost kitschy. An enormous watershed moment right in the nick of time and suddenly everything is okay. And he knows that’s how it sounds. "I always said I had no expectations from this trip. But that’s not true. I wanted to find something. I was looking for redemption.”
The story could end here. But there’s more.
In the afternoon, the bus is struggling its way through the hills. Edgerton and the others have just visited a decommissioned U.S. air base. It is the final hours the group will spend in the region where Edgerton was deployed.
Suddenly, Edgerton calls out: "Stop!” He jumps up and rushes to the window. Outside, only jungle can be seen. But one of the hills, the tallest of them all, seems different. Its shape isn’t quite right. Flat on top, like a volcano.
"That’s Fuller,” Edgerton says. "My fire base. That’s where I was.” One of the five hills where he spent several months of his life. Where he directed fire at a country about which he knew nothing and wanted to know nothing.
Half a century later, the hill is still there. Green and covered in vegetation. Nature has taken it back
Edgerton wipes the tears from his face. "Let’s go.”
